title: Babarvani close
hookLine: faith that doesn't look away from suffering

lines: A NURSE LOOKS AT THE WOUND.
THE PAIN NAMED, THE WOMEN MOURNED.
cards: A nurse changing a dressing doesn't look away from the wound. She looks closely and steadily, because looking is part of the care. Turning away would be easier, and it would help no one.

For days now this path has read Guru Nanak's hymns on Babur's invasion: the pain named, the women mourned, the truth told to Lalo. Today they close, with one question. What does a faith look like that keeps its eyes open?

teach.h: FIRST, THEY LOOK: THE PAIN IS NAMED.
teach.b: Babarvani is the name given to these hymns. Look back over what they do, and three things stand out. First, they look.
They don't hurry a massacre into a tidy lesson. They stay with the dust, the broken homes, the ordinary people who paid for a war they never chose.
The hymn on ang three hundred sixty even turns to God and asks, in paraphrase: there was so much slaughter, such crying, and did You feel no pain?
Second, they keep calling God the Master. The same hymn names the Creator as the Master of all. Protest and trust share a single breath: a question like that is only asked of someone who is there.

teach.h: THE HYMNS ARE KEPT IN SCRIPTURE.
teach.b: Third, they're kept. These aren't private notes hidden in a drawer. They sit in the Guru Granth Sahib, in Raga Asa and Raga Tilang, inside the same scripture that sings of joy and praise.
A gathering can sing of the Beloved's beauty and, from the same pages, of a town that burned. So faith, in these hymns, isn't a way of looking away.

teach.h: FAITH THAT ASKS, AND STILL TRUSTS.
teach.b: It looks at the worst thing it can see, names it, grieves it, and brings the question straight to God, still saying God's name while it asks.
That's today's line: faith that sees.

how: The Babarvani hymns are part of the Guru Granth Sahib and are sung in kirtan and explained in katha, where they are heard as Guru Nanak standing with ordinary people who suffer in war.

o: a closing prayer said when a gurdwara shuts
the end of Nanak's hymns on Babur's invasion
the treaty that ended Babur's war in Punjab

games.q: what's inside the hymns — tap the pairs.

s: the Babarvani hymns stop calling God the Master
the same hymn that cries out also names the Creator as the Master of all.
the hymn on ang 360 asks God, did You feel no pain?
so much slaughter, such crying: the question goes straight to the Creator.
the hymns hurry past the suffering to a lesson
they stay with it: the dust, the broken homes, the crying.

games.q: these hymns describe a town that burned. where are they kept?
o: in a history book, apart from the hymns of praise.
in the Guru Granth Sahib, beside hymns of joy and praise.
nowhere; they were sung once and dropped.
games.why: they sit in scripture, in Raga Asa and Raga Tilang, in the same pages that sing of joy, and they're still sung.

practice: Bring to mind one hard thing you usually glance past, far away in the news or close by, on your own street or in your own house, and just look at it for a few breaths without fixing it or explaining it away.

If you pray, bring it to God plainly, as a question if it is one; if you don't, simply let it be seen. And if the hard thing is danger to you or someone close, reach for help now: 988 in the US, or your local emergency number.

wordCard.voice: Babarvani close. The end of Guru Nanak's hymns on Babur's invasion: they name the suffering, grieve it, and still call God the Master. Today's word.

orig.note: babarvani: the name for Guru Nanak's hymns on Babur's invasion; the word also appears in one of them.

carryVoice: Your line: faith that sees. The Babarvani is closed, but its eyes stay open. See you tomorrow.
